phase_0.name: RMI-00043767
phase_0.feature: Cache Purging
phase_0.business_value: App performance; case reduction
phase_0.risks_and_dependencies: Depends on Komaci priming consolidation with briefcase rules (XL).
phase_0.description:
Brief

The mobile app does not delete records from the local cache, even if they are no longer needed or have been deleted from the server. This leads to bloated space, and can lead to issues where the mobile device stores old/stale data.


Customer Impact

  1. Bloated space of device: as high volume briefcases grow and we start to prime binaries (images, files, ai models, maps, etc), it is increasingly important to remove primed data we no longer need. App storage usage will bloat, db size will grow (performance will slow), and the only way to fix these problems is to uninstall the app.
  2. Stale data: CONA reported an issue where their LWC picklists pull from all available data. When they delete records from the server, the mobile app keeps these records (because we do not do cache purging). Thus, they see extra fields that should not exist. This is a usability issue, and can also lead to errors where a technician attempts to use a record that does not exist or they do not have access to anymore.


Goal

Delete/purge records from the local cache when they are no longer needed.


Definition of “No longer needed”:

When a record or binary would not be primed again upon the user deleting and re-installing the app, it can be classified as “no longer needed”. Equivalently, only records that should actively be primed to the device from the various priming stages should be saved. This does not need to be instant, but can be a sweep every x hours/days. Eg: a record does not need to be purged the instant it is removed from a briefcase.


Concern

From HLD: If we begin consuming out-of-scope records from the Priming Service in 260, there’s a significant risk of unintentionally deleting records that are still required by LWC components. This gap in visibility poses a serious concern and could lead to critical data being removed prematurely.


Resolution Options

  1. From HLD: “As a temporary solution until we fully transition to Briefcase as the single source of truth, we can implement a cache purging strategy using a combination of out-of-scope records from the Priming Service and the sObject Get Deleted API.”
  2. Only implement cache purging when “Turn Off Komachi Priming for LWCs” is enabled (thus LWC records are tracked in briefcase and out of scope will always apply)
  3. Wait for Komaci on server initiative  


260 Decision

Enhance clear cache metadata button to fully clear mobile cache (including LDS DB and all other content except login state). Then force a full reprime. This will wipe the cache and re-download.


Customers can use this as often as needed and tell technicians to use it on a schedule.


Key Feedback: We need to ensure this doesn’t clear the upload queue or else it will cause cases.

Solution: This button should only be active when the upload queue is empty. 


HLD Link HLD - 260 - Performance Priming


Planning Discussion

Start

Tracking db cache size, query time over time

Button to force full reprime (and clear entire cache) (UX design may exist), don’t allow spamming


Ideas

  • Ability to clear cache and do full reprime without logging out
  • Visibility into cache size 
  • “We recommend clear cache” -> call to action
  • TTL on last read, delete record if hasn't been read in X days

phase_0.name: RMI-00043763
phase_0.feature: LDS Record Indexing - Index all standard tables / queries
phase_0.business_value: App Performance
phase_0.description:
Brief

LDS is the platform data store layer for the field service mobile app (when enabled). It allows us to build on top of the platform for features like agentforce, but can lead to slowness when record volumes grow. This is partially due to the fact that the LDS database is non-indexed, so queries on large data sets are slow.


Customer Impact

We are force migrating customers to LDS over the next year, so more customers will be migrated to LDS. It is known that LDS causes slowness, and this is a contributing factor. 


Fisher and Pickel see mobile app queries to LDS cache taking 357.5568ms vs a projected 0.4292ms with indexing. This is up to a 99.88% decrease in query time for EVERY operation on the mobile app. 100ms is the threshold where users start to perceive lag/delay, so this change is the difference between an app that feels laggy and one that feels perfectly instantaneous and responsive.


Goal

Auto indexing for common fields. In 260, this is manual


See More

Engineering PRD PRD: LDS DB Indexing Optimization on Field Service

phase_0.name: RMI-00043785
phase_0.feature: Low Network Connectivity Indicator (Feasibility)
phase_0.business_value: Top Customer Complaint - driving case load
phase_0.description:
Know Your Connection — Low-Connectivity Awareness for Field Service Mobile (1 Pager)

Workstream: Mobile Experience Author: Andrew Little Date: 2026-06-25 Status: DraftOne-line summary: When the network gets weak, Field Service Mobile tells the technician plainly, explains what it means for their experience, and offers a one-tap switch into the app's existing offline mode until the connection recovers.

1. Press Release

Headline: Salesforce Field Service Mobile now recognizes a weak connection and tells the technician — so a slow app is never a mystery.

Subhead: For field technicians working in basements, elevators, and remote sites, the app now explains why it's slow and lets them choose a steady offline experience instead of fighting a spinner.

Body:

The problem. A technician opens a work order in a mechanical room with one flickering bar. The screen spins. They can't tell whether the app is broken, their phone is the problem, or it's just the signal — so they wait, force-quit, or call the office. Today the app only knows "online" or "offline," so a connection that's technically up but painfully slow looks like a frozen app with no explanation. The setting that would let them take control is buried in Advanced Settings, where no one looks mid-job.

What we shipped. The app now recognizes when you're in a low-connectivity environmentand says so, right where you're working, with a calm, non-blocking message. Tap to learn what it means — which actions may be slow, what's still fully available on your device, and that your work is safe. And if the slowness isn't worth waiting through, you can switch to offline mode in one tap for a steady, predictable experience using your downloaded data — then switch back, or let the app prompt you, the moment a good connection returns.

The customer quote. "Before, my techs thought the app was broken when it was really just a dead zone — now they know it's the signal, and they can flip to offline and keep moving instead of standing there waiting on a spinner," said Maria Delgado, Field Operations Manager at a national HVAC service company.

Availability. Targeted for release 266 on iOS and Android. No new license tier required — it builds directly on the app's existing offline mode and connectivity detection, and honors the org's current settings.

2. The customer & the problem

Persona(s): Field Technician (primary); Dispatcher (secondary — benefits when techs choose offline rather than appearing stuck or unresponsive).

Job to be done: When my app is slow and I don't know why, I want to understand that it's the network — not a broken app or lost work — and decide how to proceed, so I can keep working without frustration or wasted waiting.

Today's pain (specific, observed): Connectivity is modeled as binary (online/offline) on both platforms. A connection that's up but unusably slow is treated as "online," so the app appears to hang while it waits on server round-trips, with no explanation. The only place to take control is a "force offline" toggle buried in Advanced Settings — invisible mid-job. The technician can't tell a dead zone from a broken app, and has no in-context way to opt out of the slow experience. Workaround: wait on the spinner, force-quit, or call the office.

Evidence this is real:

  • Sync/connectivity issues are the #1 customer-trust liability — the largest share of mobile customer-impact support cases and the longest average resolution time (mobile-worker-trust/index.html, 2026).
  • "Connectivity expectation-setting" is explicitly named as a next lever for the sync-trust target (same source) — i.e., the gap is awareness, not just faster sync.
  • Only ~0.7–1% of page views are fully offline (2026-04-offline-usage-share-analysis.md, 2026-04-15) — proving the pain lives in the degraded middle the app doesn't yet recognize or explain.

3. The proposal

What we'd build: Two layers, in order of value.

(1) Awareness (the core — ship this unconditionally): detect a degraded connection (not just on/off) and surface a calm, non-blocking banner where the technician works — "Weak connection — the app may be slow. Your work is safe." This is the single most-cited usability principle (visibility of system status); the app already runs the connectivity probe — it just throws away the latency that would tell it "degraded" and keeps only on/off. Surfacing it is pure upside, no behavior change, near-zero risk.

(1a) Educational "learn more" (part of the core): a tap on the banner opens short, plain-language help — what a weak connection means, which actions may be slow, what's still fully available on your device, that your work is safe, and what choosing to go fully offline would (and would not) do for your experience. This is where we set honest expectations ("steady on your downloaded data, not faster"). It's cheap, it's all upside, and it lets the awareness layer stand on its own even before the offline lever exists — including pointing the technician to where offline mode and sync status already live today.

(2) Informed choice — the offline lever (STRETCH / optional, gated): when degradation is sustained, offer a one-tap switch into the app's existing offline mode for a steady, predictable experience on already-downloaded data. The offline button drives the same internal switch the Advanced Settings toggle already uses — we're surfacing an existing, tested capability in context, not building offline mode. The guardrails that make this safe are part of this layer, not optional within it: a prominent "you're offline" indicator so no one forgets the mode they're in, a proactive "connection's back — switch online?" prompt, one-tap reversibility, and suggesting offline only when the local cache is primed enough for it to actually help. This layer ships only after Layer 1 proves the problem worth it (see sizing).

Reused, explicitly not net-new: the Data Sync screen already shows per-item sync status today. We are not building per-item sync badges or a new queue view. Where it helps (e.g., from "learn more" or after switching offline), we link to the existing Data Sync screen so the technician can see what's synced — no new sync UI.

What we'd not build (out of scope):

  • A promise that offline is faster — it's predictable, and only helps for data already on the device (see FAQ).
  • Any net-new per-item sync state. It already exists on the Data Sync screen; we reuse it by linking to it, and build no new sync UI, badges, or queue view.
  • Eliminating the sync bar (the competing roadmap branch).
  • Conflict resolution, new transport tech (Multipath / Wi-Fi Aware), and dispatcher desktop surfaces.

Why this approach over the alternatives: It's purely additive — no behavior change to the online path — so it sidesteps the "indicator vs. eliminate sync bar" debate entirely. It respects the field tech as an expert user (give them the lever, don't decide for them — user control and expert-accelerator best practice) while keeping a calm default. And by reusing the existing offline toggle's plumbing, it stays small.

The one trap we must not fall into: offline only helps when the slow data is already cached locally. If the technician needs data that hasn't been downloaded, switching offline turns a slow load into a dead end — making trust worse, not better. So the promise is always "a steady, predictable experience on your downloaded data," never "go faster." This is why the offline switch is offered when the cache is primed, not blanket-pushed whenever the signal dips.


Proposal: https://salesforce.enterprise.slack.com/docs/T0257US1S/F0BD4048DM1

  • $105M AOV affected by Service Reports and Signature Experience VOCs

Quality and Stability Comparison:

  • Service Reports 1.0: 167 total cases, 12 Sev1 incidents, 47 Sev2 incidents (59 high-priority total), 126 accounts affected
  • Document Builder 2.0: 62 bugs/investigations, 0 Sev1, 0 Sev2 incidents
  • Result: 63% fewer incidents, 100% reduction in high-priority issues

Technical Debt:

  • Service Reports 1.0 uses legacy C++ codebase and Visualforce Quote Template
  • Cannot be enhanced due to architectural constraints
  • Templates cannot deploy from Sandbox to Production
  • Limited to Work Order and Work Order Line Item objects only

CUSTOMER PAIN POINTS (Research with 23 customers)

  • 91% (21 of 23) need multiple templates per object - SR 1.0 supports only one
  • 65% (15 of 23) need Work Order level generation - SR 1.0 only supports WOLI
  • 61% (14 of 23) report stale offline preview data
  • 52% (12 of 23) need multi-language section headers - SR 1.0 supports field labels only
  • 48% (11 of 23) need professional formatting control - customer feedback: "Documents don't look professional, can't send as-is" (EATON)
  • 48% (11 of 23) need advanced template selection rules - SR 1.0 has manual selection only

MIGRATION APPROACH

Phase 1: Automated Template Conversion Tooling

  • Build conversion engine to transform SR 1.0 page layout metadata to Document Builder 2.0 flexipage format
  • Leverage Salesforce APIs for metadata transformation
  • Claude-powered migration assistance for complex template patterns
  • Automated validation to ensure template parity

Phase 2: Dual-Generation Preview Experience

  • System automatically generates both SR 1.0 and Doc Builder 2.0 versions
  • Technicians compare reports side-by-side in-field during workflows
  • Preview screen shows both versions with visual comparison
  • Embedded migration help documentation and feedback collection
  • Admin-controlled migration: only org administrators can execute the switch from 1.0 to 2.0

Phase 3: Phased Customer Rollout

  • Cohort 1: Early adopter customers already piloting Doc Builder 2.0
  • Cohort 2: High-impact customers with known pain points (multi-language, multiple templates)
  • Cohort 3: Long-tail customers with standard configurations
  • Success criteria per cohort: migration rate, feedback sentiment, incident reduction

Phase 4: Service Reports 1.0 Sunset

  • Deprecation notice with 12-month runway
  • Disable new Service Reports 1.0 template creation
  • Full platform decommission after migration completion

TIMELINE
7 quarters (21 months) phased approach:

  • Q1: 25% customer migration (Cohort 1 + early Cohort 2)
  • Q2: 60% customer migration (Complete Cohort 2)
  • Q3: 90% customer migration (Cohort 3)
  • Q4: 100% migration complete + SR 1.0 sunset

TECHNICAL FOUNDATION COMPARISON

Service Reports 1.0:

  • Legacy C++ codebase and Visualforce Quote Template
  • Cannot be enhanced
  • Limited to Work Order and Work Order Line Item objects
  • No Sandbox to Production deployment
  • One template per record
  • Limited formatting control

Document Builder 2.0:

  • Modern Salesforce platform and Lightning Web Components
  • Built for ongoing innovation and extensibility
  • Supports 6+ object types: WO, WOLI, SA, Quote, Visits, Interactions
  • Platform-native deployment capabilities
  • Multiple templates with auto-selection
  • Professional formatting: fonts, colors, positioning, branding

SUCCESS CRITERIA

Migration Metrics:

  • Q1: 25% of customers migrated
  • Q2: 60% of customers migrated
  • Q3: 90% of customers migrated
  • Q4: 100% migration complete

Quality Metrics:

  • Maintain 0 Sev1/Sev2 incidents in Document Builder 2.0
  • >95% automated template conversion success rate
  • 50% reduction in template-related support cases
  • Improved customer satisfaction (NPS)

phase_0.name: RMI-00044059
phase_0.feature: Native on the Hot Path
phase_0.description:
Native LDS on the launch-critical ("hot") path. Replace the JavaScript LDS/Luvio data layer with a native implementation so record reads run in-language (Swift on iOS) against SQL, rather than in a single-threaded JSContext worker bridged over JSValue. Native GraphQL/SOQL record query is the beachhead; the strategic end-state is retiring the JS worker from the launch path entirely.

Why it matters (measured): the JS LDS/LMR stack round-trips Swift↔JSValue on every emission, serializes all adapter calls on one worker thread, and stores data as a single (key, JSON) blob table scanned in JS. Native replaces all three at once: concurrent WAL readers, a real SQL planner (WHERE/ORDER BY/JOIN), and typed Swift snapshots with no bridge hop.

phase_0.name: RMI-00043876
phase_0.feature: OS Minor-Release Regression Guard (iOS/Android)
phase_0.description:
Why

iOS minor OS updates have twice caused regressions in our application experience that we did not catch before the OS shipped to customers:

  • A JavaScript rendering engine change caused a high crash rate for several critical customers.
  • A security enhancement in a minor release broke deep linking.

Both were discovered only after the OS update reached customers, forcing reactive hotfixes instead of proactive detection.

Proposal

Run our regression suite against the upcoming minor releases of both iOS and Android ahead of general availability, using developer/public betas, so we can spot OS-induced regressions before the OS ships and get ahead of customer impact.

Outcome

Early-warning signal on OS minor releases for both platforms, reducing reactive post-release firefighting and protecting critical customers from OS-induced regressions.

phase_1.name: RMI-00043768
phase_1.feature: Process briefcase predicates with relative date predicates to fix current date range limitation
phase_1.description:
This is a documented limitation, so we are covered, but this could have really high impact on customers which are only looking at "today" service appointments.


See limitations: https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.mfs_perf_priming_limits_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5


"Delta priming for future-scheduled service appointments or service document templates may experience a delay of up to 24 hours. This delay occurs because the system checks for existing matches only one time every 24 hours. However, we check new records immediately via Change Data Capture. For example, if an admin configures the system to prime service appointments up to 7 days in the future:

  • An appointment scheduled 7.1 days away doesn't initially meet the 7-day criteria.
  • After 24 hours, the system re-checks. If the appointment is then 6.1 days away, it falls within the filter criteria and is primed.
  • As a result, an appointment could be within the future window (for example, between 6.1 and 7.0 days away) but it isn't primed until the next 24-hour check. This delay can be more significant with shorter priming windows; for a 2-day window, an appointment isn't primed until it’s 1.1 days away.

This delay impacts the "Future Days in the Date Picker" and "Days After Current Service Date" settings within Field Service Mobile Settings."

phase_1.health_comments: Officially paused 28 Apr 2026 (FY27 Q1 V2MOM) to free capacity for higher-value work. Discovery complete; revisit pending PG&E/PubSec demand + SKU/Promon pricing resolution.
phase_1.description:
Summary

Evaluate porting the Salesforce Mobile App Plus (MAP+) Security SDK — also called the Enhanced Mobile App Security (EMAS) SDK — into the Field Service Mobile app. It is a platform-level library giving enterprises MAM (Mobile Application Management) controls. Today it ships as a separate SKU (part of SApp+) and is not included in Field Service. Primary driver: PG&E (PubSec / DoD / Gov Cloud), with similar BYOD-contractor demand from SApp financial and HLS customers.

Status

🛑 Officially paused on 28 Apr 2026 in the FY27 Q1 V2MOM review, to free capacity for higher-value work. Substantial discovery already complete (PRD, gap analysis, tech estimate).

Key Capabilities the SDK Enables

  • Jailbreak / root detection and device block
  • Block screenshots and screen recording (Android; detection-only on iOS)
  • Block copy/paste of app data
  • Minimum OS and app version enforcement
  • Certificate pinning and MITM detection
  • Offline policy enforcement (policies cached and enforced without network)
  • Audit logging of security events (MobileEnforcedPolicyEvent, MobileScreenshotEvent, MobSecurityCertPinEvent, etc.)

Third-party dependency: the SDK uses Promon for some enforcement policies. Salesforce has an existing Promon contract; adding SFS usage requires negotiating an expanded license and determining where the costs land.

Engineering Estimate

Directional (30 Sep 2025, reviewed by Nitish Khadiya & Saket Agarwal): 8–10 weeks SFS engineering + 4–5 weeks Mobile Platform. Risks: maintenance burden, binary-size impact for all customers (even non-users), and Promon licensing.

Discussion Timeline

  • 18 Sep 2025 — First signal: DoD / Gov Cloud push; LFI contact saw FS as a major DoD push (Battles).
  • 28 Sep 2025 — Battles requests an LOE to integrate the SDK for PG&E; add to Customer Requested Features.
  • 29 Sep 2025 — Graham Oldfield looped in; initial tech questions (iOS Objective-C codebase flagged).
  • 30 Sep 2025 — Engineering estimate provided (8–10 + 4–5 weeks).
  • 2 Oct 2025 — PG&E confirms MAM (not MDM) needs: block copy/paste, block screenshots, jailbreak detection. SKU/pricing/Promon complexity flagged.
  • 4 Dec 2025 — Gap analysis built: 95%+ coverage if EMAS ported. Minor gaps: iOS screenshot blocking (OS limit), auto cache-purge timers (mitigable).
  • 11 Feb 2026 — Field Service Mobile Security SDK PRD created (competitive analysis: Oracle MAF vs. MAP+).
  • 6–25 Mar 2026 — Gap analysis refined across teams; validating current SFS support.
  • 20 Mar 2026 — Exec team briefed; Andrew named cost-estimation lead.
  • 13 Apr 2026 — PCT review; Andrew Shand engaged to correct the gap analysis.
  • 28 Apr 2026 — Work officially paused.
  • 20 Aug 2026 — Technical doc on Logging in Mobile Security SDK (iOS) shared (five event types).

Key Documents

  • Gap Analysis — PG&E Security Requirements (95%+ coverage confirmed)
  • Field Service Mobile Security SDK PRD (competitive analysis; PG&E primary driver)
  • Rough Tech Eval and Estimate
  • Salesforce Mobile App Security: Intune vs. Mobile App Plus
  • Logging in Mobile Security SDK (iOS)
  • Salesforce Help: Enhanced Mobile App Security

Open Considerations

  • Pricing & Packaging — SDK is part of SApp+ (MAP+); SFS would need a new SKU or licensing arrangement.
  • Promon licensing costs — third-party library costs need resolution and allocation.
  • Build vs. buy — some PG&E requirements (e.g. block copy/paste) may already exist natively in SFS; full audit recommended.
  • iOS limitations — screenshot blocking not possible on iOS; only detection and logging.
  • Binary size — integration affects all SFS customers, not just SDK users.
  • Broader market validation — PubSec (DoD/gov), HLS, and BYOD contractor demand; design-partner validation recommended before building.

phase_1.name: RMI-00043761
phase_1.feature: UI for delay on mobile from error code
phase_1.description:
This was part of 258 UX design but was never implemented due to lack of capacity. Slowdowns in briefcase/core job execution may cause Sync in Progress to spin for a long time, and technicians want feedback that the system is under heavy load.


We had a case where this impacted SCE go-live recently.
